# Paddle

Claim

Paddle is a London-based merchant-of-record platform that sells, bills, and remits sales tax on behalf of digital product and SaaS companies across more than 300 markets, combining checkout, subscription billing, fraud protection, and ProfitWell subscription analytics under one platform.

## About This Company

## Introduction

Paddle is a payments and subscription-billing platform that acts as the merchant of record for digital product and SaaS companies. Instead of stitching together a payment processor, tax engine, subscription tool, and dunning service, a Paddle customer routes its transactions through Paddle.com Market Limited, which appears on the buyer’s statement, handles the card acquiring, calculates and remits sales tax in the buyer’s jurisdiction, and forwards the net proceeds to the seller. The London-based company describes itself as “the Merchant of Record that empowers digital product companies to operate and grow, automatically,” and positions its platform as a single back-office for software businesses that sell across more than 300 markets. Through the 2022 ProfitWell acquisition it also bundles subscription metrics, retention analytics, and dunning into the same platform, giving founders and finance teams a unified view of revenue, churn, and tax exposure.

## History & background

Paddle was founded in 2012 in London by Christian Owens and Harrison Rose, with Owens taking the chief-executive role and Rose serving as co-founder in customer-facing leadership positions over the company’s first decade. The legal entity, Paddle.com Market Limited, was incorporated at Companies House on 8 August 2012 under company number 08172165 and remains registered at Judd House, 18-29 Mora Street, London EC1V 8BT. The company spent its early years building a checkout and licensing layer aimed at independent software vendors and gradually expanded into subscription billing, tax compliance, and fraud protection. In May 2022 Paddle raised a $200M Series D round that valued the company at $1.4B, taking total funding raised to $293M and earning it unicorn status in the United Kingdom.

## Mission & vision

Paddle’s stated mission is to let software businesses run and grow their subscription operations automatically, by absorbing the operational and regulatory work that normally sits between a SaaS company and its customers. The vision the company articulates on its homepage is “Sell globally. Grow without the complexity”: a digital product company should be able to launch in a new country without separately registering for VAT, contracting an acquirer, or wiring up a churn-recovery flow. Paddle’s role, as it describes it, is to “do it for you” rather than “help you solve it” — taking responsibility, as merchant of record, for the contracts, tax filings, and compliance work that come with cross-border digital sales, so that engineering and finance teams inside the seller can stay focused on product and revenue.

## Products & services

Paddle’s platform is structured around a payments and billing core wrapped with revenue and retention tooling. Paddle Billing handles subscription plans, trials, proration, and dunning. Checkout provides hosted and overlay flows with support for a wide range of payment methods. Payments and Tax & Compliance work together to acquire transactions, then register, collect, file, and remit sales tax and VAT on the seller’s behalf across digital-goods jurisdictions. Invoicing covers B2B SaaS flows where buyers need purchase orders and bank-transfer settlement. Fraud Protection screens transactions and manages chargebacks. From the ProfitWell side of the platform, ProfitWell Metrics provides subscription analytics such as MRR and churn, while Retain automates failed-payment recovery to reduce involuntary churn. An In-app Purchase product extends the same merchant-of-record model to mobile apps as an alternative to the platform stores.

## Technology & approach

Technically, Paddle is a hosted platform that integrates into a seller’s product through a JavaScript checkout, server-side APIs, and webhooks. The company maintains developer documentation at developer.paddle.com and publishes SDKs and reference integrations for common stacks. Its architectural choice is to operate as the merchant of record rather than a payment-facilitator or pure payment-processor: the contract of sale sits between Paddle and the buyer, which is what allows Paddle to take on tax-collection, refund, and chargeback liability for the seller. The platform processes a high volume of digital-goods transactions across hundreds of markets and routes them through multiple acquirers and alternative payment methods to optimise authorisation rates. Subscription analytics, billing, and dunning are exposed through the same dashboard and APIs that handle checkout, so finance and growth teams work from a single source of truth.

## Target audience

Paddle’s natural customer is a software business that sells a digital product or subscription, especially one that wants to sell internationally without standing up an in-house finance, tax, and compliance team. That includes independent software vendors, indie SaaS founders, growing scale-ups, and larger digital-content businesses operating across many jurisdictions. The company has historically focused on SaaS, downloadable software, and digital subscriptions; its in-app purchase product extends the same model to mobile developers. Buyers inside customer organisations are typically founders, finance leaders, and engineering leaders who weigh Paddle against in-house combinations of payment processors, tax services, and subscription tools, and against competitors such as Stripe Billing, Lemon Squeezy, FastSpring, and Chargebee.

## Unique value proposition

The distinct claim Paddle makes is that one contract with a single supplier replaces a stack of payments, tax, billing, fraud, and retention tools — and that Paddle, not the seller, takes on the regulatory and operational liability for that stack. For a software company that wants to sell into multiple countries, this removes the need to register for VAT in each jurisdiction, contract with multiple acquirers, or wire together a separate dunning system. Customers retain commercial control of pricing, packaging, and product, while Paddle stands between them and the payment networks, tax authorities, and buyers. The platform’s bundling of ProfitWell-derived analytics with merchant-of-record billing is the other distinguishing claim: revenue, retention, and tax data sit inside the same operational layer rather than being scattered across separate tools.

## Strengths & advantages

Operational scope is Paddle’s main advantage. Because Paddle is the merchant of record, it absorbs tax registration, filing, and remittance work that a seller would otherwise have to take on country by country, and it handles refund and chargeback flows under its own merchant relationships. Its homepage cites large headline volumes — figures including 190 million transactions processed, $130 million in sales taxes remitted annually, 10,000+ customers, and 6,000+ active businesses — which suggest meaningful scale across digital-goods payments. The 2022 ProfitWell acquisition adds a credible subscription-analytics and retention layer to the same platform, giving Paddle a wider footprint than a pure payments competitor. The product set is broad enough that many SaaS sellers can run their commercial back office on Paddle end-to-end, without contracting a separate tax engine or analytics tool.

## Market presence & achievements

Paddle has grown from a UK startup into a privately held company with around 280 employees per its own About page (LinkedIn places it in the 201-500 employee band), with offices in London and New York. The May 2022 Series D round of $200M valued the company at $1.4B and made it one of the UK’s most recent software unicorns; the same month it announced the $200M acquisition of Boston-based ProfitWell, then in use by more than 30,000 businesses. Total disclosed funding stands at $293M from investors including KKR, FTV Capital, and BGF. Customers Paddle has cited publicly include Fortinet, Framer, Iconosquare, Renderforest, Matomo, MacPaw, and a portfolio of ProfitWell-era SaaS brands that became Paddle customers through the acquisition. Beyond the 2022 fundraise and acquisition, no further 2023-2026 funding round, IPO, or major M&A event has been publicly disclosed.

## Trust & compliance

Trust posture matters more for Paddle than for most software companies, because the company sits inside the regulated payments and tax-collection path. Paddle publishes security and compliance information through a dedicated portal, with references to SOC 2 and GDPR as part of its public security material. As merchant of record under Paddle.com Market Limited, the company holds the tax-registration and acquiring relationships needed to collect and remit sales tax and VAT for digital goods across more than 300 markets, which is the regulatory backbone of the product. Buyer-side support is routed through paddle.net for transaction questions, and seller-side support through the in-app dashboard chat. The company’s UK legal entity carries Companies House number 08172165 and LEI 2549003RPFV2JYJACF51, giving it a public identity for compliance and counterparty checks.

## Considerations & challenges

There are practical considerations a prospective customer should weigh before standing up on Paddle. Because Paddle is the merchant of record, it appears on the buyer’s statement and owns the customer-payment relationship, which is a structural trade-off compared with directly contracting an acquirer through a tool like Stripe Billing. Pricing is not publicly listed on the website and is negotiated per customer, which means evaluation requires a sales conversation rather than a public pricing comparison. Paddle does not publish a general contact email address or phone number — support is handled through the in-product dashboard chat — which can be friction during initial vendor due diligence. Headline customer counts and tax-volume figures are vendor-reported and not separately audited. Finally, no major new funding round, IPO, or acquisition has been disclosed for 2023-2026, so prospective customers evaluating long-term direction are working from the 2022 Series D / ProfitWell announcements plus subsequent product communications.

## Conclusion

Paddle is a London-based merchant-of-record platform that consolidates payments, subscription billing, sales-tax compliance, fraud protection, and (since 2022) ProfitWell-derived subscription analytics into a single operational layer for digital product and SaaS companies. Founded in 2012 by Christian Owens and Harrison Rose, with ~280 employees, $293M in disclosed funding, and the 2022 ProfitWell acquisition behind it, the company sells the proposition that one supplier can replace the payments-and-billing stack a SaaS business would otherwise have to assemble itself. For software companies that want to sell internationally without taking on tax registration, acquiring contracts, and dunning infrastructure in-house, Paddle is built to do that work as the merchant of record; the trade-offs to weigh are the structural role it plays on the buyer’s statement, the absence of public pricing, and the limited public disclosures since the 2022 fundraise.
